A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ControlValve research. Their main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, with retained material identifiable across appendix reordering and table renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original attack-success and benign-performance experiments on CFH-Hard, accidental security violations, and graph-generation evaluations across three models.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds AgentDojo Slack experiments, runtime measurements, and observed rule-generation failure modes.

M1.justification: ControlValve's grammar generation, contextual edge rules, parser and LLM enforcement, and three-attempt replanning procedure remain unchanged. The Slack integration is described as an evaluation wrapper; no change to the defense algorithm is documented.

E1.justification: V2 adds actual evaluation on all 21 AgentDojo Slack tasks, including information exfiltration through fake support tickets and a Slack CFH input. V1 used AgentDojo attack presentations but did not evaluate its task environment. The existing ten coding and six computer-use CFH-Hard tasks are retained.

E2.justification: Tables 1-3 retain the undefended system, Azure Content Filters, least privilege, and LlamaFirewall with the same four table-labelled backing models. V2's Slack attack comparison extends this comparator set to the new benchmark. Its runtime comparison also uses existing methods.

E3.justification: Sections 5-5.2 change the reported orchestrator, answer judge, and one LlamaFirewall backing model from o4 to o4-mini. V1's tables already label that LlamaFirewall variant o4-mini, so these edits do not establish reruns. V2 also introduces the custom Slack evaluation setup and a runtime metric averaged only over successful rollouts.

E4.justification: New Appendix D analyzes three execution failure modes: unnecessary human intervention, hallucinated tools, and hallucinated URLs under overly restrictive rules. Appendix E adds an empirical runtime comparison. These introduce substantial analysis of operational failures and efficiency beyond the retained graph-generation ablation, now Appendix C.

E5.justification: Existing task experiments retain three trials, and the graph-generation ablation retains five generations per task. The new Slack and timing results follow the existing three-trial averaging practice. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or experimental seed information.

E6.justification: V2 adds Slack CFH attack-success rates of 0% for ControlValve versus 40%-56% for LlamaFirewall variants (Table 5), and benign success of 62% versus 65% undefended (Table 6). Table 9 adds successful-rollout times of 128 seconds for ControlValve, 51 undefended, and 86-107 for LlamaFirewall. Matched pre-existing result tables retain their numerical values.

T1.justification: The context-free-grammar formulation, example CFG, and graph-quality definitions remain unchanged. V2 introduces no new formal assumptions, mathematical derivations, theorems, or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion are unchanged. The central claims about alignment-check evasion, ControlValve's contextual control-flow defense, and accidental security violations are retained. AgentDojo supplies additional supporting evidence, while orchestration-only operation with black-box agents was already specified in v1.

C2.justification: V1 broadly acknowledges overly restrictive graphs and rules. V2 connects restrictive rules to specific human-intervention and hallucination failures, and adds runtime feasibility as a limitation (Section 4; Appendices D-E). Appendix B also interprets the new 62% versus 65% benign scores as preserving utility.

D1.justification: V2 documents a custom AgentDojo wrapper with two Slack-interface agents and newly states that unnecessary human intervention counts as failed execution. Existing CFH-Hard task prompts, attack payloads, execution traces, and CFG/rule examples remain available under the revised appendix organization.

R1.justification: The bibliography, Section 7, and Appendix A are unchanged. Section 4 adds a specific applicability argument against tool-call policing such as Shi et al. (2025b): remote agents' API calls cannot be intercepted in the assumed deployment. This modestly sharpens the defense's research positioning.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites clarify black-box deployment, limitations, and experimental setup. The dataset subsection is broadened, appendix results are grouped before task and payload listings, and the publication header is updated. The main section structure and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds compact Slack attack, Slack utility, and runtime tables (5, 6, and 9). Existing benign-result tables are relocated together as Tables 10-11, and some captions are refined. The four figures remain unchanged, and the existing table style and single-column layout are retained.

improvement.justification: V2 materially strengthens evaluation beyond the authors' CFH-Hard tasks through the adapted AgentDojo Slack benchmark, while addressing previously unmeasured execution costs and concrete rule-generation failures. The additions make practical security claims more assessable: zero observed attack success accompanies 62% versus 65% benign success and 128 versus 51 seconds on successful rollouts. These tradeoffs improve transparency rather than merely adding favorable results. Uncertainty estimates remain absent and timing excludes failures, but the broader validation and operational analysis substantially improve the paper's evidential basis.
